card: Three of Gladiolus · Three of Swords
notes: Tone-under-load card. Held the line on: no promise it passes, no reframe, no advice. The 'rain as weather, not cleansing' move in libraryEntry A feels like the strongest thing here.

readingLine: Three blades through one shape, and rain drawn in straight lines. Something true landed, and it landed sharp. The accuracy is what makes it ache — a miss would have been easy to shrug off. Nothing here asks you to feel better yet.

Rain on the plate, and it isn't decorative. This is the card of the sentence that went in clean — said to you, or by you, or finally admitted. It hurts in proportion to how true it is, which at least makes it information.
question: What did this hurt say plainly that kindness kept blurry?
Which sentence went in clean, and who said it?
libraryEntry: Three blades, one pierced shape, rain ruled in straight engraver's lines. Of all the cards in the deck this one hides the least: something hurt, and it hurt because it was accurate. Vague blows glance off. The sentences that stay are the ones with your exact address on them — said by someone who knows you, or said by you, quietly, after a long time not saying them. The card doesn't ask you to reframe any of that. Rain on a specimen plate isn't a symbol of cleansing; it's weather, drawn honestly, falling on a thing that got cut. What the card notices is only this: precision and cruelty aren't the same, even when they arrive in the same sentence. Some part of the hurt is the truth's edge, and some part is how it was handled, and untangling those two is slow, sober work. The sentence itself, written down, tends to come out smaller than the one that's been circling the room.

The suit of Gladiolus does its thinking in blades, and here three of them meet in one place, with rain. This is the deck's plainest card about pain: not disaster, not betrayal necessarily — accuracy. A true thing touched a sore thing, and the two turned out to be the same size. People reach for anesthetic readings here, and the card politely declines to provide one. It doesn't say the rain ends. It doesn't say the wound teaches. It says: this is what a direct hit looks like, drawn without shading, and you're allowed to call it what it is. There's a dignity in that, the same dignity the plate gives its specimens — labeled, unprettified, seen. Grief over a truth is still grief, and it keeps grief's schedule, not yours. What the card offers is a dry place to stand for two minutes: the sentence named, the entry point noted, and the naming allowed to be enough for today.
altText: Three narrow blade leaves crossing one point, straight rain lines behind, on a pale plate.
Engraving of three sword-lily leaves meeting at a pierced center, rain ruled diagonally.
reversedReadingLine: The blades are out, mostly. What's left is the ache of a truth you've already absorbed — old rain, still falling in one corner of the week. Some hurts get kept past their honesty, and this one may be asking, mildly, to be done.

Rain easing without quite stopping. Reversed, the sharp sentence is behind you but still quoted often, word for word, with the emphasis polished. The wound closed; the retelling keeps its office hours. There's a difference between remembering a thing and staffing it.
reversedQuestion: What would be missing if you stopped retelling this one?
Which old sentence do you still recite with fresh emphasis?
reversedLibraryEntry: Reversed, the three blades hang loose in the shape they once pierced. The event is over. The sentence was true, or true enough, and it did what true sentences do; what remains is curation — the retelling, the anniversary observances, the way the story has developed reliable beats. None of this is shameful. Some hurts were formative, and a formed thing keeps its mold's shape long after the mold is gone. The card only notices when tending a scar turns into staffing a museum: guided tours daily, exhibits dusted, admission charged to whoever gets close to you. The rain in the image has mostly passed, which is exactly why the remaining drizzle stands out. Old grief kept on retainer stops being grief and becomes a schedule. Somewhere under the retelling sits the original, smaller sentence, the one that actually happened. Visited occasionally, without the exhibit lighting, it tends to shrink back to the size it was.

There's a second way this card lands reversed: the truth arrived and was never granted entry. The sentence got said — by a friend, a colleague, the year itself — and was met at the door, thanked, and turned away. The blades in the image can hang in the air a long time like that, neither in nor gone. Meanwhile the weather stays unsettled. Small irritations arrive with strange force; unrelated conversations keep drifting toward one topic and being steered back. That's the unabsorbed truth, billing you by the week. Absorbing it is not the same as agreeing with all of it. Most sharp sentences are partly right, and the part that's right is usually smaller than it sounded at full volume. Once the accurate fraction is let in and the exaggerated remainder filed, the sky tends to settle — accounts closed, weather ordinary again, and the week's small irritations back to their actual size.
